articles.title: Nestlé Will Strip Artificial Colourings From Every Product on Earth by Year-End — and It Could Reshape What Indians Eat
articles.excerpt: The Swiss food giant becomes the first major packaged-food company to set a global deadline for eliminating synthetic dyes, a move driven by GLP-1 drug pressure and RFK Jr.'s FDA crackdown that could ripple through Maggi, KitKat, and Munch in India
articles.image_caption: Nestlé products on a supermarket shelf — the company plans to remove all artificial colourings from its global portfolio by end-2026
articles.nri_angle: NRIs navigating different food safety standards between the US/UK and India may finally see consistency as Nestlé standardises its ingredient lists globally — including for iconic Indian brands like Maggi and KitKat
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Simultaneous Heat Emergency Is Scorching Two Continents — and Millions of Indian Diaspora Are in Its Path
articles.excerpt: Europe's deadliest heatwave in years has killed over 1,300 people, and now a punishing heat dome is descending on the US for July 4th. For the 7 million-strong Indian diaspora across both regions, the message is the same: this is not normal summer heat.
articles.image_caption: Extreme heat conditions — a simultaneous heatwave is affecting both the United States and South Asia (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Over 6 million Indian-origin residents in the US and UK face record-breaking heat in their home cities, with multigenerational households and elderly family members at acute risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A New Weight-Loss Drug Just Matched Bariatric Surgery — and It Could Change How South Asians Fight Obesity
articles.excerpt: Eli Lilly's retatrutide produced 28% weight loss at 80 weeks in the landmark TRIUMPH-1 trial, the first medication ever to rival surgical outcomes — a potential game-changer for a community with the world's highest metabolic disease burden.
articles.image_caption: An Ozempic injection pen — retatrutide belongs to the same GLP-1 drug class but targets three metabolic receptors instead of one
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry the world's highest metabolic disease burden relative to BMI — a drug matching bariatric surgery outcomes could transform obesity treatment for the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Weedkiller in Your Food May Be Rewiring Your Brain Through Your Gut — and the 'Safe' Doses Aren't So Safe
articles.excerpt: A wave of new research finds glyphosate — sprayed on wheat, oats, lentils, and most American crops — disrupts gut bacteria, alters brain chemistry, and triggers anxiety-like behavior at doses far below regulatory limits
articles.image_caption: Agricultural spraying in a crop field — glyphosate is the world's most widely used herbicide
articles.nri_angle: NRIs face high glyphosate exposure through the American food supply — and India's own use of the herbicide on tea, wheat, and lentils means the risk cuts across both food systems
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Medicare Will Now Cover Ozempic and Wegovy for Weight Loss — Here's Who Qualifies and What It Costs
articles.excerpt: A new pilot program launching July 1 lets eligible seniors get GLP-1 drugs for just $50 a month, but the fine print matters — and the clock is already ticking.
articles.image_caption: An Ozempic (semaglutide) injection pen — Medicare will now cover GLP-1 medications for weight loss (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: South Asians face elevated metabolic risk at lower BMI thresholds, and many NRI families are navigating Medicare coverage for aging parents — making this program particularly relevant for multigenerational Indian American households.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: South Asians Have the Highest Heart Disease Risk at 45 — Despite Eating Better and Drinking Less Than Everyone Else
articles.excerpt: A decade-long study of 2,700 U.S. adults found that South Asian men and women develop prediabetes, hypertension, and high cholesterol earlier than every other racial group — even though they report healthier diets and lower alcohol use. The researchers say visceral fat and early-life exposures may explain the paradox.
articles.image_caption: A doctor checks blood pressure during a cardiovascular screening — researchers say South Asians should begin heart health screenings before midlife
articles.nri_angle: South Asian Americans face the highest cardiovascular risk of any U.S. racial group by age 45 — a finding that demands earlier screening, lipoprotein(a) testing, and culturally tailored care for the diaspora community.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Walking 10,000 Steps a Day Can Offset a Full Day at Your Desk, a 72,000-Person Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Researchers at the University of Sydney found that each increase in daily steps — up to about 10,000 — was linked to a 39% lower risk of death and 21% lower risk of heart disease, regardless of how many hours participants spent sitting. For the millions of South Asian tech workers who log 8-plus hours at a desk, the data offers a clear prescription.
articles.image_caption: Walking remains the most accessible countermeasure to prolonged sitting, with benefits scaling up to about 10,000 steps per day
articles.nri_angle: South Asian tech workers in the U.S. spend 8-10 hours at desks — among the highest sedentary rates of any demographic — and already face elevated cardiovascular risk by midlife. Walking 10,000 steps daily can meaningfully offset the damage.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Americans Are Ditching Multivitamins for Targeted Supplements — and Two of the Fastest-Growing Are Ayurvedic Staples
articles.excerpt: A 25-year JAMA analysis of 63,000 adults finds supplement use surging while multivitamin use drops — with turmeric and ashwagandha leading the charge
articles.image_caption: Assorted dietary supplements including vitamin D, magnesium, and turmeric capsules
articles.nri_angle: Turmeric and ashwagandha — Ayurvedic staples in South Asian households — are now among America's fastest-growing supplements, while targeted vitamin D matters disproportionately for NRIs at higher latitudes.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The FDA Just Cleared an AI Tool That Detects Hidden Heart Disease From a Routine ECG — and South Asians May Benefit Most
articles.excerpt: EchoNext, trained on 700,000 ECG records, caught severe heart failure a cardiologist missed — and its clearance could reshape screening for high-risk populations
articles.image_caption: An electrocardiogram readout showing heart rhythm patterns
articles.nri_angle: South Asians face 2-4x higher coronary disease rates and often develop heart disease a decade earlier — an AI tool that reads hidden cardiac risk from routine ECGs could catch disease years before symptoms appear.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Strength Training Cuts Type 2 Diabetes Risk by Up to 62% — and Consistency Matters More Than Intensity
articles.excerpt: A study of nearly 144,000 people over 19 years found that regular weight training — especially when combined with cardio and less screen time — offers powerful diabetes protection that South Asians have extra reason to pay attention to.
articles.image_caption: A woman performing strength training exercises in a gym studio
articles.nri_angle: South Asians are genetically predisposed to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes at lower BMIs — making the case for strength training even more urgent for the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Gut Bacteria May Reveal Colorectal Cancer Before Symptoms Appear — and Fiber Could Be the Key to Prevention
articles.excerpt: A new study in Cell Host & Microbe has identified a consistent microbial signature linked to colorectal cancer across ages and populations — and lower fiber intake made it worse.
articles.image_caption: Illustration of the human gut microbiome, increasingly linked to colorectal cancer detection and prevention (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Colorectal cancer rates are surging among young adults globally, and NRIs shifting from fiber-rich Indian diets to Western ultra-processed food face particular risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: GLP-1 Drugs Like Ozempic Are Now Linked to Smell and Taste Disturbances — and the Implications Go Beyond Food
articles.excerpt: A study of nearly 900,000 diabetes patients found that GLP-1 users had an 81% higher risk of smell dysfunction and a 52% higher risk of taste changes — subtle shifts that doctors say are early markers of neurological health.
articles.image_caption: A semaglutide injection pen — GLP-1 receptor agonists like Ozempic are now linked to smell and taste disturbances in a growing body of research (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: South Asians have among the highest GLP-1 prescription rates due to elevated type 2 diabetes prevalence, and sensory loss carries outsized cultural weight in communities where food is central to identity.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Exercise Alone Can Address Six of the 14 Modifiable Risk Factors for Dementia, a New Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Researchers at the University of Minnesota say consistent physical activity can prevent or delay up to half of all dementia cases — and a telehealth pilot proved it works even in rural communities with no gym access.
articles.image_caption: Regular physical exercise is increasingly shown to reduce modifiable risk factors for dementia, including in older adults (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: South Asians face elevated dementia risk through high rates of diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease — making the case for exercise as neuroprotection especially urgent for the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The FDA Just Said There's 'Little Evidence' Behind the Peptides Millions of Americans Are Injecting
articles.excerpt: BPC-157, TB-500, and five other peptides popular in wellness circles face a July FDA review — while the advisory panel itself includes sellers and promoters of the same compounds.
articles.image_caption: Peptide compounds in a laboratory setting, increasingly popular in wellness circles
articles.nri_angle: Health-conscious Indian Americans are among early adopters of peptide therapies marketed through wellness influencers; the FDA review signals these unproven compounds carry real risks.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Fish Oil Supplements Don't Protect Your Brain From Alzheimer's, a Rigorous Two-Year Trial Confirms
articles.excerpt: A USC Keck School of Medicine study found that high-dose omega-3 reached the brain but failed to improve memory, prevent cell loss, or slow cognitive decline — upending the $1 billion supplement industry's core claim.
articles.image_caption: Fish oil capsules, one of the most popular dietary supplements in the United States
articles.nri_angle: South Asians face higher Alzheimer's risk factors and widely use fish oil supplements; this study shows supplements alone won't protect the brain.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Americans Now View Ultra-Processed Foods as Addictive as Alcohol — and a Bipartisan Majority Wants the Government to Act
articles.excerpt: A landmark Cornell survey of 2,000 adults finds rare bipartisan consensus: over 60% see UPFs as a major cause of obesity, diabetes, and heart disease, with parallels to tobacco drawing calls for regulation that could reshape what NRI families eat in America.
articles.image_caption: Packaged ultra-processed snacks and beverages on a supermarket shelf
articles.nri_angle: South Asian immigrants in the US consume significantly more ultra-processed foods than their traditional diets would include, and the community already faces elevated risks of diabetes and heart disease — making this policy moment directly relevant to NRI health.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: 80% of People Aren't Getting Enough of the Nutrient That Protects Hearts and Brains — Even If They Eat Their Five a Day
articles.excerpt: A 30,000-person urine analysis published in Food & Function found that fewer than one in five people consume the 500mg daily flavanol target linked to slower cognitive decline and lower cardiovascular risk — and the fix may be as simple as a cup of green tea.
articles.image_caption: Fresh berries and green tea are among the richest dietary sources of flavanols
articles.nri_angle: South Asian diets rich in green tea, pomegranates, and amla offer a natural flavanol advantage — but processed-food shifts among NRIs may be eroding it precisely when their elevated cardiovascular risk makes it most important.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Switching to E-Cigarettes After Quitting Smoking May Nearly Double Your Lung Cancer Death Risk, a 4.5-Million-Person Study Finds
articles.excerpt: The largest study of its kind, published in Nature Medicine, tracked former smokers for five years and found that those who switched to daily vaping had a 56% higher lung cancer incidence and a 100% higher lung cancer death risk compared to those who quit completely.
articles.image_caption: E-cigarettes contain formaldehyde and toxic metals that may contribute to lung cancer risk
articles.nri_angle: India banned e-cigarette sales in 2019, but vaping rates among Indian-American teens are rising — this 4.5-million-person study raises urgent questions about cancer risk for a generation picking up vaping as a first habit, not a cessation tool.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Millennials and Gen Z Are Aging Faster Inside Their Bodies — and It May Be Fueling a Cancer Surge
articles.excerpt: A landmark study of 164,000 people across the US and UK found that younger generations show significantly more biological 'wear and tear' than their parents did at the same age — and the gap is linked to rising early-onset cancers in the gut, lungs, and uterus.
articles.image_caption: A researcher examines blood biomarker data in a laboratory setting
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry elevated metabolic and inflammatory risk factors that accelerate biological aging — this study adds urgency to earlier screening and lifestyle intervention for young NRI professionals.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Brain Starts Calming Down in Just Two Minutes of Meditation — and Peak Zen Arrives at Seven
articles.excerpt: A Harvard and NIMHANS brain-scan study mapped exactly when meditation rewires your neural activity — and even complete beginners showed the same timing as seasoned practitioners
articles.image_caption: A person meditating — researchers found the brain begins calming within two to three minutes
articles.nri_angle: NIMHANS-Harvard collaboration bridges Indian contemplative traditions with Western neuroscience, offering busy NRI professionals a research-backed seven-minute prescription for stress relief
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nearly Half of Adults Over 65 Actually Got Sharper With Age — and Their Mindset Was the Key
articles.excerpt: A Yale study tracking 11,000 Americans for 12 years found that positive beliefs about aging predicted real improvements in cognition and physical function — not just slower decline
articles.image_caption: An elderly couple walking together in a park — the Yale study measured physical improvement through walking speed
articles.nri_angle: NRIs watching parents age from afar can take heart: positive attitudes about aging are not just cultural values but measurable health interventions, and the conversations families have across continents may shape real outcomes
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Hormone Therapy Slashes Osteoporosis Risk by 69% — and South Asian Women May Have the Most to Gain
articles.excerpt: A new study presented at ENDO 2026 adds to growing evidence that menopausal hormone therapy protects bone density. For South Asian women — who face earlier menopause and higher fracture risk — the findings carry extra urgency.
articles.image_caption: A bone density scanner used to check for osteoporosis. (Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.0)
articles.nri_angle: South Asian women experience menopause earlier on average and have higher baseline bone resorption rates, making HRT's bone-protective benefits especially relevant for NRI women and their mothers back home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Remote Work Is Making People Lonelier — and the Effects Are Worst for Those Living Alone
articles.excerpt: A landmark study of 588,000 workers published in Science found that remote work accounts for roughly a third of the post-pandemic rise in mental distress. For NRI tech workers far from family, the findings hit close to home.
articles.image_caption: A person working alone from home on a laptop
articles.nri_angle: NRI tech workers — many of them remote, many living alone thousands of miles from family — face a compounded version of the isolation this study describes, with immigration-related social barriers layered on top.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: GLP-1 Poison Control Calls Have Surged Fivefold — and a New Pill That Doesn't Require Fasting Could Change Everything
articles.excerpt: A Journal of Medical Toxicology study reveals over 10,000 GLP-1 exposures reported to U.S. poison centers, while a new oral drug published in Nature Medicine shows 16% weight loss with no empty-stomach requirement — developments that matter deeply for the South Asian diaspora.
articles.image_caption: An Ozempic (semaglutide) injection pen, the GLP-1 drug that now accounts for 64% of all poison control calls in this drug class
articles.nri_angle: South Asians have among the highest global rates of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome, making them one of the fastest-growing demographics on GLP-1 drugs in the US — and disproportionately affected by both the safety risks and the promise of cheaper oral alternatives.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A New Blood Test Catches 90% of Aggressive Prostate Cancers That the Standard PSA Misses — and Only 6% of Men Are Even Being Screened
articles.excerpt: The Stockholm3 test, validated in a 12,000-man trial published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, detected aggressive prostate cancer far more reliably than the decades-old PSA — a breakthrough that matters for South Asian men who face cultural barriers to screening.
articles.image_caption: Blood test tubes in a medical laboratory — the Stockholm3 test uses a single blood draw to detect aggressive prostate cancer
articles.nri_angle: South Asian men in the US often delay or avoid prostate screening due to cultural stigma around the exam, and prostate cancer is the second most common cancer in men globally — this blood test could remove one of the biggest barriers to early detection.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Type of Fat in Your Kitchen May Matter More Than How Much You Use — and a New Review Shows Why
articles.excerpt: Palmitic acid, the dominant saturated fat in ghee, palm oil and processed snacks, drives insulin resistance at the molecular level. Oleic acid — abundant in olive oil and mustard oil — may reverse it. A University of Barcelona review in Trends in Endocrinology & Metabolism lays out the evidence.
articles.image_caption: A bottle of extra-virgin olive oil, rich in oleic acid, which a new review links to lower insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes protection
articles.nri_angle: South Asians have the highest insulin resistance rates in the world, and the palmitic-acid-heavy fats in traditional Indian cooking — ghee, palm oil, vanaspati — are now directly implicated at the molecular level.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Gut Bacteria May Explain Why Coffee Wrecks Your Sleep — and a 7,000-Person Study Just Mapped the Connection
articles.excerpt: A Nature Communications study of nearly 7,000 Dutch adults found 137 bacterial species linked to sleep quality. Two Clostridia species appear to mediate coffee's effect on social jet lag — the gap between your weekday and weekend sleep clocks.
articles.image_caption: A freshly brewed cup of coffee — a new study finds gut bacteria may mediate its disruptive effect on sleep timing
articles.nri_angle: South Asians are heavy coffee and chai consumers, and NRI tech workers face extreme social jet lag from cross-timezone schedules — gut microbiome differences could amplify or mitigate these effects.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Leafy Greens in Your Thali May Be Quietly Protecting Your Lungs — and a Major New Study Shows How
articles.excerpt: Researchers tracked 179,000 adults for over a decade and found that those who ate the most vitamin K1 — abundant in spinach, kale, and methi — had a 16% lower risk of chronic lung disease.
articles.image_caption: Fresh leafy greens including spinach, kale, and other vitamin K1-rich vegetables
articles.nri_angle: Indian cuisine's rich tradition of leafy greens — palak, methi, sarson, bathua — provides among the highest vitamin K1 intakes of any food culture, offering NRIs a familiar dietary tool to protect lung health.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: One in Four Depression Cases May Be Driven by Inflammation — and Standard Antidepressants Often Don't Work for Them
articles.excerpt: Growing evidence points to a distinct subtype of depression fuelled by chronic inflammation, with implications for South Asians who carry higher metabolic and inflammatory risk.
articles.image_caption: Emerging research links chronic inflammation to a distinct subtype of depression that resists standard antidepressant treatment
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry elevated baseline inflammation from metabolic syndrome at higher rates than any other ethnic group, meaning NRIs may be disproportionately affected by inflammation-driven depression — and less likely to respond to standard SSRIs.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
